title: Clark Terry
summary: Johnson describes Terry's sound, humor and reputation as an educator.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: You had a group around this time with Sonny Stitt and Clark Terry, a group that toured Japan. You spoke a little bit about Sonny Stitt. I know you have very warm feelings for Clark Terry, and I was wondering if you could speak a little about him.

The brilliant Clark Terry. The first time I ever heard about Clark Terry was the word of mouth that was getting around in jazz circles that he sounded like a combination of Dizzy, Miles and Clifford Brown all rolled into one. I couldn’t imagine such a player. And yet, when I first heard him, I thought, "That’s pretty accurate. That’s pretty on target." He is a cross between Dizzy, Miles and Clifford Brown. Yet he has his own persona and his own style that is uniquely Clark Terry that transcends this combination of Dizzy, Miles and Clifford Brown. It was a wonderful experience to finally hear him and meet him as a person because, as we all know, he is a fun guy with a tremendous sense of humor. A real sharp guy. A real bright guy and I’m told, by reliable sources, a very good jazz educator.

One of the best. The word is that he really does a number when he does a clinic or a workshop or a master class. It's masterful, shall we say. Da-da-da-dah. To hear you say that, Dave, just seconds the motion as to what I’ve heard by word of mouth, that he is one of the best.
He was on the ground floor of the whole movement.
